Lecture 35: The Cost Model of the Web

Interview Question

CORE

What is web performance, and what is the cost model of the web?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Zoe launches the National Times digital subscriber campaign on a high-speed office fiber network.
  2. The redesign renders rich hero graphics, animated widgets, and three megabytes of client scripts.
  3. Field telemetry reveals forty percent of mobile subscribers on cellular connections bounce immediately.
  4. Why does an eight-second mobile load time destroy subscriber conversions despite pristine desktop testing?
  5. The team measured performance on high-end hardware without calculating the physical cost model of the web.
  6. Ignoring network latency and client CPU constraints creates bloated applications that alienate mobile readers.
  7. Today we analyze round-trip time, calculate the true cost of JavaScript, and optimize the web performance budget.

The Bandwidth Illusion: Why More Megabits Do Not Fix Latency

Zoe reviews real-user telemetry to understand why rural subscribers abandon the National Times checkout flow. When engineering teams test web applications on gigabit corporate Wi-Fi, they mistake network bandwidth for network speed. While high bandwidth allows massive video files to download quickly, initial page delivery is constrained by round-trip latency (RTT), TCP handshakes, and slow-start congestion windows. On high-latency mobile networks, shipping hundreds of small external requests forces the radio to idle across sequential round trips:

resource-payload.html
1<link rel="stylesheet" href="/style-bundle-2mb.css" />
WRONG: 2MB blocking stylesheet stalls mobile radio
2
3<link rel="stylesheet" href="/style-core-18kb.css" />
RIGHT: 18KB critical styles fit in initial TCP bursts
Mobile Payload: Bloated 2MB Bundle vs 18KB Streamlined Core
WRONG: 2MB BLOATED PAYLOAD
Subscription Landing
✕ 8.4s LCP on 3G · 40% bounce rate
RIGHT: 18KB CRITICAL PAYLOAD
Subscription Landing
✓ 1.2s LCP on 3G · Fast mobile conversion

The contrast illustrates why bandwidth cannot overcome latency. Because the speed of light in optical fiber is limited to roughly 200 kilometers per millisecond, physical distance imposes an irreducible round-trip delay. When a browser initiates a new connection, it must perform DNS resolution, a TCP three-way handshake, and a TLS cryptographic negotiation before requesting the first byte. Under TCP slow-start, the server delivers the initial response in a small congestion window of approximately 14 kilobytes. On the left, downloading two megabytes requires dozens of round-trip network acknowledgments, stranding the mobile user on an empty screen. On the right, keeping critical styles under 18 kilobytes delivers the complete layout within the very first network burst.

The Heavy Byte: Why JavaScript Costs More Than Images

In the cost model of the web, not all network bytes impose equal burdens on the client device. A one-megabyte JPEG photograph is streamed to the GPU, decoded off-thread, and painted without freezing the user interface. Conversely, a one-megabyte JavaScript bundle monopolizes the browser's single main thread as the V8 engine parses tokens, compiles abstract syntax trees, and executes initialization logic:

script-budget.js
1import { FullChartsSuite } from 'all-charts-3mb';
WRONG: 3MB library monopolizes main thread compilation
2
3import { renderSparkline } from './sparkline-4kb.js';
RIGHT: 4KB micro-script compiles in under 5 milliseconds
CPU Execution Cost: 3MB Monolithic Library vs 4KB Micro-Script
WRONG: 3MB SCRIPT COMPILATION
Interactive Chart
✕ 1,800ms main thread lockup (poor INP)
RIGHT: 4KB MICRO-SCRIPT
Interactive Chart
✓ 12ms main thread parse (smooth INP)

A byte of code demands far more computing resources than a byte of media. After downloading, an image requires simple decompression and memory allocation. JavaScript, however, undergoes a grueling multi-stage compilation pipeline. The browser must parse the raw text into an Abstract Syntax Tree, compile bytecode, and execute instructions on the CPU's primary execution thread. On mid-tier and budget smartphones, compiling three megabytes of script locks the main thread for nearly two full seconds, causing buttons to ignore taps and gestures to stutter. Replacing bloated libraries with focused utility functions protects the main thread and keeps user interactions fluid.

Author and web performance engineer Ilya Grigorik defines this fundamental optimization principle:

In any complex system, a large part of the performance optimization process is the untangling of the interactions between the many distinct and separate layers of the system, each with its own set of constraints and limitations.

Ilya Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking, resources/web-performance/hpbn/primer-on-web-performance/index.html

Key Takeaway

Performance is user retention; round-trip latency and main thread CPU execution cost far more than raw network bandwidth.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: contrast byte economics across media types: an image costs network transfer and GPU rasterization, while JavaScript costs transfer, decompression, lexical parsing, bytecode compilation, and main thread execution. Cite the rule of thumb that 170KB of gzipped JavaScript equates to roughly 1MB of raw code, which can consume over a second of CPU time on a mobile device before the user can tap an interactive element.

Where you will meet this

  • Cellular subscription funnels: optimizing assets so pages display content within the first two network round trips.
  • Investigative news reporting: delivering breaking dispatch reports rapidly across degraded rural mobile connections.
  • E-commerce product showcases: loading hero photos without blocking the main thread with unnecessary tracking scripts.
  • Third-party analytics auditing: identifying unoptimized marketing tags that choke mobile device memory and battery life.

Glossary

  • Cost Model of the Web: The analytical framework evaluating how network latency, bandwidth, CPU parsing, and battery power limit performance.
  • Round-Trip Time (RTT): The duration required for a network packet to travel from the browser to the server and return.
  • TCP Slow-Start: A congestion control algorithm where the server begins transmission with a conservative burst (initcwnd) before scaling up.
  • Main Thread Contention: The bottleneck that occurs when intensive JavaScript compilation blocks user taps and rendering updates.
  • Byte Inequality: The reality that script bytes demand orders of magnitude more device computation than equivalent image bytes.

Summary

Network Physics and Client Execution Economics

Web performance is governed by immutable physical laws and device constraints. Upgrading server bandwidth cannot eliminate round-trip latency, and downloading huge JavaScript payloads overtaxes budget mobile processors. Design for high-latency cellular connections, respect the initial TCP packet window, and minimize main thread execution debt. Here is your streetwise review.

❒ The Core Laws of the Web Cost Model

  1. Network Transmission Laws
        (a) RTT dominates mobile load times; latency cannot be resolved by raw bandwidth.
        (b) Keep initial critical payloads under 14KB to fit within TCP initcwnd.
        (c) Minimize connection handshakes by terminating SSL at CDN edge nodes.
  2. Client Compute Constraints
        (a) Treat JavaScript as the most expensive asset on the web.
        (b) Account for mobile CPU thermal throttling and memory limits.
        (c) Ship lightweight functional code and defer non-critical analytics.

DO NOT DO THIS: Ship massive uncompressed script bundles that freeze mobile devices.

index.html
1<script src="/bundles/analytics-heavy-v1.js"></script>
2<link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/global-everything.css">

    DO THIS: Ship lean critical assets and stream non-essential code asynchronously.

index.html
1<link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/critical-core.css">
2<script defer src="/bundles/app-minimal.js"></script>

➔ NEVER assume field users possess desktop CPUs or gigabit fiber connections.

➔ ALWAYS fit critical initial render assets inside the initial 14KB TCP burst.

➔ IF evaluating asset weight THEN budget JavaScript at 5x the cost of equivalent images.

file transfer speed		Round-trip latency (RTT)

Lecture 36: The Critical Rendering Path

Interview Question

CORE

What is the critical rendering path from HTML to paint, and what blocks it?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Julian inspects the morning investigative lead story on the National Times website.
  2. The web server returns the initial HTML document across the wire in under fifty milliseconds.
  3. Julian stares at a stark white screen for three full seconds before any text or photo appears.
  4. Why does the browser refuse to paint text despite possessing the complete HTML markup?
  5. The document head linked an enormous uncompressed CSS stylesheet that blocked the render tree.
  6. Render-blocking stylesheets and parser-blocking scripts stall browser pipelines and leave screens completely blank.
  7. Today we trace the critical rendering path, eliminate blocking stylesheets, and deliver instant First Contentful Paint.

The White Screen Freeze: Why CSS Blocks Initial Paint

Julian opens the morning transit dispatch on his phone, expecting instant editorial text. When a browser downloads an HTML document, it builds the Document Object Model (DOM) by parsing tokens into nodes. However, the browser cannot render text immediately because content requires styling rules to determine font sizes, layout bounds, and visibility. External stylesheets linked in the document head are render-blocking by default; until the CSS Object Model (CSSOM) is constructed, the screen remains completely white:

blocking-css.html
1<link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/mega-bundle.css" />
WRONG: 400KB external CSS blocks initial render
2
3<style>body{font-family:serif;margin:0;padding:16px;}</style>
RIGHT: Inlined critical styles paint instantly
First Contentful Paint: Render-Blocking CSS vs Inlined Critical Styles
WRONG: RENDER-BLOCKING CSS
Morning Transit Report
✕ 3.2s blank white screen (stalled FCP)
RIGHT: INLINED CRITICAL CSS
Morning Transit Report
✓ 0.4s instant typography paint (fast FCP)

The contrast exposes the core bottleneck of the critical rendering path. On the left, the browser encounters <link rel="stylesheet">, pauses construction of the render tree, and initiates an external HTTP network fetch. If cellular network conditions are poor, Julian waits through several round trips of pure white screen time before a single letter renders. On the right, embedding the minimal CSS required for above-the-fold reading directly into an inline <style> block allows the browser to construct the DOM and CSSOM concurrently from the initial HTML stream, painting the editorial headline in under half a second.

The Render Tree Pipeline: From DOM and CSSOM to Layout and Paint

The browser converts raw bytes into pixels on screen through a deterministic five-stage pipeline: DOM construction, CSSOM construction, Render Tree synthesis, Layout computation, and Paint rasterization. Crucially, the Render Tree combines only visible nodes from the DOM with matching styles from the CSSOM. Elements declared with display: none or scripts that execute synchronously alter this pipeline, forcing the layout engine to calculate exact geometric coordinates before passing pixels to the GPU:

parser-scripts.html
1<script src="/analytics/tracker.js"></script>
WRONG: Synchronous script halts HTML tokenizer
2
3<script defer src="/analytics/tracker.js"></script>
RIGHT: Defers execution until DOM parses
Parser Pipeline: Synchronous Script vs Deferred Non-Blocking Execution
WRONG: SYNC SCRIPT PAUSED DOM

Headline: Route 9 Overpass Reopens

✕ HTML parsing paused for script fetch
RIGHT: DEFERRED SCRIPT PIPELINE

Headline: Route 9 Overpass Reopens

✓ DOM tree streams without pause

The presence of JavaScript in the critical path introduces a dual dependency. Because scripts can query and mutate both the DOM (via element creation) and the CSSOM (via computed styles), encountering a plain <script> tag forces the browser to halt HTML tokenization immediately. Even worse, if an external stylesheet is downloading concurrently, script execution must pause until the CSSOM finishes building. Deferring non-critical scripts eliminates this pause, allowing the HTML parser to build the DOM uninterrupted.

Web performance pioneer Ilya Grigorik defines the critical rendering path in the official Google documentation:

Optimizing the critical rendering path refers to prioritizing the display of content that relates to the current user action.

Ilya Grigorik, Critical Rendering Path, resources/web-performance/web-dev/src/site/content/en/blog/critical-rendering-path/index.md

Key Takeaway

CSS is render-blocking and JavaScript is parser-blocking; optimize First Contentful Paint by inlining critical styles and deferring scripts.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: recite the exact five stages of the Critical Rendering Path: (1) DOM construction from HTML tokens, (2) CSSOM construction from stylesheets, (3) Render Tree construction pairing visible DOM nodes with computed styles, (4) Layout calculating the exact pixel geometry and coordinates of each box, and (5) Paint rasterizing pixels onto the GPU display buffer. Highlight how display: none excludes elements from the Render Tree, whereas visibility: hidden keeps elements in Layout and Paint.

Where you will meet this

  • Above-the-fold news delivery: inlining critical typography and grid styles to achieve sub-second First Contentful Paint.
  • Single-page application entry points: scoping root HTML payloads so empty shell containers render before massive bundles load.
  • E-commerce product showcases: preventing blank product page screens by deferring non-essential rating and review stylesheets.
  • Print stylesheet optimization: using media="print" on print stylesheets so they download in the background without blocking screen paint.

Glossary

  • Critical Rendering Path (CRP): The sequence of steps the browser performs to convert HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into pixels on screen.
  • CSS Object Model (CSSOM): A tree of style nodes derived from CSS rules, detailing computed styling for every DOM element.
  • Render Tree: The combination of visible DOM nodes and matching CSSOM rules used to compute layout geometry.
  • Layout (Reflow): The computational phase determining the exact physical width, height, and viewport coordinates of every box.
  • Paint (Rasterization): The final process of converting layout boxes into actual colored pixels on the user's screen.

Summary

Pipeline Architecture and Render-Blocking Mitigation

A fast web experience depends on streamlining the journey from HTML bytes to painted pixels. Render-blocking stylesheets and synchronous scripts freeze the browser engine, leaving users staring at blank white viewports. Inline above-the-fold critical CSS, defer non-essential scripts, and protect the render tree from unnecessary pipeline stalls. Here is your streetwise review.

❒ The Five Milestones of the Critical Rendering Path

  1. Construction Milestones
        (a) DOM: parses HTML bytes into document object model nodes.
        (b) CSSOM: parses CSS rules into style declarations; blocks rendering.
        (c) Render Tree: merges visible DOM nodes with CSSOM computed styles.
  2. Rendering Milestones
        (a) Layout: calculates geometric box dimensions and viewport positions.
        (b) Paint: rasterizes layout boxes into pixels across compositing layers.
        (c) Defer non-critical CSS with media="print" or async link loading.

DO NOT DO THIS: Link large external stylesheets in the head that stall the render tree.

index.html
1<head>
2 <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/mega-bundle-global.css">
3 <script src="/scripts/third-party-tracker.js"></script>
4</head>

    DO THIS: Inline minimal critical styles and defer third-party scripts.

index.html
1<head>
2 <style>h1{font-size:24px;}body{margin:0;padding:12px;}</style>
3 <script defer src="/scripts/third-party-tracker.js"></script>
4</head>

➔ NEVER place synchronous JavaScript tags before external stylesheets in the document head.

➔ ALWAYS inline above-the-fold critical CSS directly into the initial HTML document.

➔ IF a stylesheet applies only to print or wide viewports THEN specify the media attribute.

RENDER-BLOCKING CRP
(unoptimized head)		STREAMLINED CRP
(inlined critical path)

browser waiting on CSS		Instant typography;
FCP under 500ms

external stylesheet RTT		Constructs CSSOM from
inline HTML styles

and waits for CSSOM		Runs deferred after
DOM tree is built

on mobile cellular		Achieved within the
first TCP network burst

loading experience		Snappy, immediate, and
professionally engineered

Lecture 37: Script Loading: Async Versus Defer

Interview Question

CORE

What is the difference between async and defer, and where should scripts go?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Maya monitors the morning news dispatch as editors publish an emergency transit bulletin.
  2. The marketing team adds an external conversion tracking script directly into the document head.
  3. Subscribers loading the breaking report stare at a frozen screen while the script downloads.
  4. Why does adding one external script freeze document rendering across the entire website?
  5. The plain script tag paused the HTML parser and blocked the main thread until the remote server answered.
  6. Synchronous scripts in the head halt document parsing and inflate Time to First Contentful Paint.
  7. Today we master async and defer attributes, evaluate execution order, and unblock the browser pipeline.

The Parser Freeze: Why Plain Scripts Halt HTML Tokenization

Maya reviews customer drop-off metrics on the National Times breaking news portal. By default, when a browser's HTML parser encounters a standard <script src="..."> tag, it must stop immediately. It cannot know whether the external script intends to invoke document.write() or modify the DOM tree, so tokenization halts while the network fetches the file and the engine executes it. If the third-party server suffers network latency, the entire webpage freezes in an unrendered state:

parser-blocking.html
1<script src="https://ads.vendor.com/tracker.js"></script>
WRONG: Blocks HTML parser and freezes rendering
2
3<script async src="https://ads.vendor.com/tracker.js"></script>
RIGHT: Downloads in background without pausing parser
Head Script: Parser-Blocking Freeze vs Non-Blocking Async
WRONG: PLAIN SCRIPT TAG
Breaking Transit Alert
✕ 2.8s parser freeze waiting on network
RIGHT: ASYNC SCRIPT TAG
Breaking Transit Alert
✓ 0ms parser pause; streams in background

The contrast illustrates the devastating impact of synchronous head scripts. On the left, every byte of subsequent HTML, including editorial headlines and lead paragraphs, is blocked from parsing until the third-party tracking script completes its round trip. On the right, adding the async attribute instructs the browser to download the script in the background on a helper thread. The HTML tokenizer continues parsing the document without pausing, allowing Maya's readers to absorb critical news while the tracking script downloads harmlessly in parallel.

Execution Guarantees: When to Deploy Async Versus Defer

Choosing between async and defer depends entirely on script dependencies and document timing requirements. Both attributes download scripts asynchronously without blocking the HTML parser. However, an async script executes the exact millisecond its download finishes, interrupting the HTML parser mid-stream and executing out of source order. In contrast, a defer script waits until the entire HTML document is parsed, executing in strict source code order just before the DOMContentLoaded event fires:

script-attributes.html
1<script async src="/app/framework.js"></script>
2<script async src="/app/components.js"></script>
WRONG: Async executes out of order, breaking dependencies
3
4<script defer src="/app/framework.js"></script>
5<script defer src="/app/components.js"></script>
RIGHT: Defer preserves exact source order
Script Timing: Async Race Condition vs Defer Ordered Execution
WRONG: ASYNC OUT OF ORDER
Component Framework
✕ Components ran before framework loaded
RIGHT: DEFER ORDERED EXECUTION
Component Framework
✓ Framework executed first, then components

Because async scripts execute whenever they arrive, smaller scripts often race ahead of larger ones. If a component library finishes downloading before the core framework, runtime exceptions throw and application initialization crashes. Defer is the universal standard for primary application scripts: it guarantees that all scripts execute in the exact order they appear in the HTML source, and only after the full DOM tree is safely constructed. Reserve async exclusively for independent, standalone scripts like Google Analytics or error monitors that have zero dependencies on other scripts or the DOM.

Web performance engineer Ilya Grigorik defines the script blocking problem in the official Google performance guides:

JavaScript allows us to modify just about every aspect of the page: content, styling, and its response to user interaction. However, JavaScript can also block DOM construction and delay when the page is rendered.

Ilya Grigorik, Adding Interactivity with JavaScript, resources/web-performance/web-dev/src/site/content/en/blog/critical-rendering-path-adding-interactivity-with-javascript/index.md

Key Takeaway

Use defer for application scripts that depend on the DOM or each other; use async only for independent third-party utilities that do not care about execution order.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: summarize the three loading behaviors in one sentence: plain scripts download and execute synchronously while pausing the HTML parser; async scripts download in parallel and execute immediately upon completion (interrupting the parser and running out of order); and defer scripts download in parallel, execute in source order after the DOM is fully parsed, and finish before DOMContentLoaded.

Where you will meet this

  • Third-party advertising tags: loading tracking pixels and affiliate beacons with async so they never delay news articles.
  • Production application bundles: loading vendor libraries and component scripts with defer to preserve initialization sequence.
  • Independent telemetry agents: deploying Sentry error logging or performance observers with async to start monitoring immediately.
  • Modern ES module loading: leveraging <script type="module"> which automatically defers execution until DOM parsing completes.

Glossary

  • Parser-Blocking Script: A synchronous script tag that halts HTML tokenization until the file is downloaded and executed.
  • async Attribute: A boolean attribute instructing the browser to download the script in parallel and execute it immediately upon arrival.
  • defer Attribute: A boolean attribute instructing the browser to download in parallel and execute in source order after DOM parsing finishes.
  • DOMContentLoaded: The browser event that fires when the initial HTML document has been completely parsed into the DOM.
  • Execution Race Condition: The bug that occurs when an async dependent script executes before its prerequisite parent library has loaded.

Summary

Asynchronous Script Delivery and Parser Optimization

Unmanaged JavaScript tags in the document head stall browser engines and degrade user retention. Eliminate synchronous script tags from the critical rendering path. Understand the fundamental behavioral divide between immediate, out-of-order async execution and orderly, post-parse defer sequencing. Here is your streetwise review.

❒ The Script Loading Decision Tree

  1. Standard Application Scripts
        (a) Always apply defer to primary frontend bundles and modules.
        (b) Guarantees execution in the exact order declared in the HTML source.
        (c) Fires reliably after the DOM tree is constructed, before DOMContentLoaded.
  2. Independent Third-Party Beacons
        (a) Apply async to analytics, heatmaps, and error monitoring scripts.
        (b) Executes immediately upon network arrival without waiting for the DOM.
        (c) Never use async if the script relies on a library or preceding variables.

DO NOT DO THIS: Place synchronous external scripts in the head, blocking the HTML parser.

index.html
1<head>
2 <script src="/bundles/main-application.js"></script>
3 <script src="/vendor/charting-library.js"></script>
4</head>

    DO THIS: Use defer to download scripts in parallel and execute them in order.

index.html
1<head>
2 <script defer src="/vendor/charting-library.js"></script>
3 <script defer src="/bundles/main-application.js"></script>
4</head>

➔ NEVER place plain synchronous <script> tags in the document <head>.

➔ ALWAYS use defer for application code that relies on DOM nodes or other scripts.

➔ IF a script is an isolated, independent tracker THEN use async for background loading.

ASYNC LOADING
(async attribute)		DEFERRED LOADING
(defer attribute)

during script run		Zero pause; parser
finishes completely

background fetch		Asynchronous; parallel
background fetch
Execution timingImmediately upon
network response		After DOM parses;
before DOMContentLoaded

downloads first		Strict source order
in the document
Recommended useIndependent beacons
and analytics		Primary application
scripts and frameworks

Lecture 38: Optimizing Images and Cumulative Layout Shift

Interview Question

CORE

How do you optimize images and prevent them from causing layout shifts?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Leo browses the morning investigative lead on his phone while riding the subway train.
  2. He taps to open an interactive transit map embedded halfway down the article page.
  3. Just before his thumb makes physical contact, the hero photo above loads and shoves the layout downward.
  4. Why did the entire page violently jump, causing Leo to click a paid advertisement by mistake?
  5. The developer omitted width and height attributes on the image, providing zero initial aspect ratio space.
  6. Unsized images trigger unexpected layout shifts that disorient readers and destroy Core Web Vitals.
  7. Today we declare explicit dimensions, reserve aspect ratio boxes, and eliminate Cumulative Layout Shift.

The Zero-Dimension Collapse: Unsized Images Versus Reserved Aspect Ratio

Leo attempts to interact with an investigative infographic during his morning commute. When an HTML document includes an <img> tag without explicit width and height attributes, the browser's layout engine has no knowledge of the image's physical proportions. Initially, the layout assigns the image container an intrinsic height of zero pixels. When the network eventually streams the image bytes into memory, the browser re-evaluates the layout tree, violently shoving all subsequent text and buttons down the screen:

image-dimensions.html
1<img src="/photos/bridge.jpg" class="hero" />
WRONG: Zero initial height forces layout reflow
2
3<img src="/photos/bridge.jpg" width="800" height="450"
4 class="hero" />
RIGHT: Reserves 16:9 box before image downloads
Hero Image Loading: Unsized Jolt vs Reserved Aspect Ratio
WRONG: UNSIZED IMAGE COLLAPSE
/photos/bridge.jpg
✕ 0px initial height · High CLS score
RIGHT: EXPLICIT WIDTH AND HEIGHT
/photos/bridge.jpg
✓ 16:9 space reserved · Zero layout shift

The contrast illustrates the root cause of high Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS). On the left, omitting dimensional attributes causes the browser to collapse the hero image container completely during initial paint. As Leo reaches out to tap the interactive map, the photo finishes downloading and expands to its natural dimensions, shifting the map four hundred pixels down and causing a mis-click. On the right, declaring width="800" and height="450" allows the browser's CSS engine to calculate an internal aspect-ratio: 800 / 450. The browser reserves the exact vertical rectangle on screen before downloading a single byte of image data, ensuring the page remains rock-solid.

Next-Gen Compression: Serving Modern Formats with the Picture Element

Preventing layout shifts ensures visual stability, but maximizing loading speed requires optimizing byte payload weight. Shipping legacy PNG and uncompressed JPEG files to mobile viewports consumes precious cellular data and delays Largest Contentful Paint (LCP). Modern image codecs like AVIF and WebP offer superior compression algorithms that reduce file size by up to eighty percent without visible quality loss. Wrapping multiple format sources in a semantic <picture> element allows user agents to select the most efficient codec supported by the client:

responsive-images.html
1<img src="/photos/hero-raw.png" />
WRONG: 3.4MB uncompressed desktop PNG sent to mobile
2
3<picture>
4 <source srcset="/photos/hero.avif" type="image/avif" />
5 <source srcset="/photos/hero.webp" type="image/webp" />
6 <img src="/photos/hero.jpg" width="800" height="450" alt="Bridge trusses" />
7</picture>
RIGHT: Next-gen formats reduce byte weight 80%
Image Formats: Legacy Heavy PNG vs Modern AVIF Picture
WRONG: 3.4MB LEGACY PNG
/photos/hero-raw.png
✕ Stalls network on 4G cellular
RIGHT: 120KB MODERN AVIF
/photos/hero.avif
✓ 85% byte savings · Sub-second LCP

The <picture> tag provides progressive enhancement across browser platforms. Browsers that support the cutting-edge AVIF format download the smallest payload possible, cutting transfer sizes down to a fraction of traditional JPEGs. Older browsers gracefully ignore modern <source> elements and fall back to the standard <img> fallback. Crucially, the fallback <img> carries the mandatory width, height, and alt attributes, ensuring accessibility and aspect-ratio reservation are preserved across all formats.

Web performance engineer Philip Walton defines Cumulative Layout Shift in the official Web Vitals specification:

Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) is a stable Core Web Vital metric. It is an important, user-centric metric for measuring visual stability because it helps quantify how often users experience unexpected layout shifts.

Philip Walton, Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), resources/web-performance/web-dev/src/site/content/en/metrics/cls/index.md

Key Takeaway

Always set explicit width and height attributes on images so browsers calculate aspect-ratio and reserve layout space before downloading.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: explain how modern browsers resolved the historical conflict between HTML dimensions and responsive CSS (max-width: 100%; height: auto;). In the past, responsive CSS overrode HTML attributes, collapsing containers to 0px until download. Modern browser engines now map HTML width and height attributes to the internal user-agent style aspect-ratio: attr(width) / attr(height), preserving aspect-ratio boxes even under responsive fluid layouts.

Where you will meet this

  • Breaking news hero packages: reserving container boxes so article text does not leap when photo assets stream in.
  • E-commerce catalog grids: stabilizing product thumbnail grids to prevent accidental taps on neighboring purchase buttons.
  • Content syndication feeds: serving AVIF images to modern Chrome and Safari users while maintaining JPEG fallbacks.
  • Editorial ad slot containers: enforcing fixed aspect ratios on programmatic ad blocks to eliminate layout shifts when banners load.

Glossary

  • Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): The Core Web Vital metric measuring the total score of all unexpected layout movements during a page lifecycle.
  • Aspect Ratio: The proportional relationship between an image's width and height, used to reserve layout space before download.
  • AVIF (AV1 Image File Format): A modern image compression standard delivering dramatic byte reductions over JPEG and WebP.
  • WebP: An efficient image format developed by Google offering lossy and lossless compression for the web.
  • Picture Element: An HTML wrapper allowing developers to declare multiple image sources tailored to format support and screen widths.

Summary

Visual Stability Architecture and Next-Gen Media Delivery

Unexpected layout shifts frustrate readers, cause accidental taps, and penalize search engine rankings. Always provide the browser with the dimensional information it needs to construct a stable layout box before network assets arrive. Couple explicit aspect ratios with modern, lightweight image formats to deliver rock-solid visual stability. Here is your streetwise review.

❒ The Visual Stability Checklist

  1. Dimensional Reservation
        (a) Always declare explicit width and height numeric attributes on <img>.
        (b) Pair with responsive CSS: img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }.
        (c) The browser computes aspect-ratio automatically, preventing layout reflow.
  2. Modern Codec Delivery
        (a) Wrap multiple codecs inside a semantic <picture> container.
        (b) Provide high-efficiency AVIF and WebP sources in priority order.
        (c) Keep standard JPEG/PNG on the inner <img> for universal fallback.

DO NOT DO THIS: Omit width and height on images, causing pages to jump when photos load.

index.html
1<div class="hero-container">
2 <img src="/photos/breaking-flood.jpg" class="responsive-banner">
3</div>

    DO THIS: Provide explicit dimensions and serve modern compressed formats.

index.html
1<picture>
2 <source srcset="/photos/flood.avif" type="image/avif">
3 <img src="/photos/flood.jpg" width="1200" height="675"
4 class="responsive-banner" alt="Flooded river">
5</picture>

➔ NEVER ship an <img> tag without explicit width and height attributes.

➔ ALWAYS wrap modern image formats in <picture> with an accessible <img> fallback.

➔ IF rendering hero images above the fold THEN do not use loading="lazy".

(reserved aspect-ratio)

to top of viewport		Exact 16:9 box reserved;
zero layout movement

megabytes of data		Next-gen AVIF/WebP;

and layout recalculation		Fast delivery;

Lecture 39: Web Font Loading: Eliminating Invisible Text

Interview Question

CORE

How do you load web fonts without causing a Flash of Invisible Text (FOIT)?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Marcus taps the breaking news notification to read the morning transit investigation.
  2. The white browser screen paints the masthead line, but the lead headline area is completely empty.
  3. Why does the article text remain completely invisible while the page has already downloaded?
  4. Marcus assumes the article failed to load and navigates away before reading a single word.
  5. The editorial typography file is still streaming across a congested cellular connection.
  6. Web fonts must display immediately using system fallbacks rather than concealing text behind blank delays.

The Invisible Headline: How Default Font Loading Blocks Content

When browsers parse CSS stylesheets containing custom web fonts, they encounter @font-face rules linked to external resource files. By default, major rendering engines hide text styled with a custom font until that font file has finished downloading across the network. This period of total visual suppression is known as Flash of Invisible Text (FOIT). On slow or lossy mobile connections, readers stare at an empty layout even though all text tokens already reside in memory:

typography.css
1font-display: block;
WRONG: Hides text for up to 3 seconds waiting for network
2
3font-display: swap;
RIGHT: Renders system fallback immediately, then swaps
Headlines: Blank Invisible Text vs Immediate System Fallback
WRONG: FOIT: 2.2S BLANK SCREEN
Morning Transit Report
✕ Invisible headline · High bounce risk
RIGHT: FONT-DISPLAY: SWAP
Morning Transit Report
✓ Immediate system font · Zero reading delay

The contrast exposes the heavy usability cost of default font blocking. Under font-display: block, the browser enters a three-second block period during which text styled with the custom family is rendered with invisible ink. If the cellular connection stalls or suffers packet loss, the headline remains an unreadable blank void. Switching to font-display: swap eliminates the block period entirely, giving it a zero-millisecond duration and an infinite swap window. The browser immediately paints the headline using the nearest local system fallback font, allowing Marcus to begin reading instantly while the custom typeface streams quietly in the background.

Accelerating Discovery: Preloading Critical Font Assets

Setting font-display: swap prevents invisible text, but swapping fonts abruptly can introduce a jarring Flash of Unstyled Text (FOUT) or Cumulative Layout Shift. Because browsers only initiate font network requests after building the Document Object Model and the CSS Object Model, font discovery typically occurs late in the critical rendering path. Preloading the critical font in the document <head> forces the browser to fetch the asset immediately during early HTML tokenization:

index.html
1<link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/typography.css" />
WRONG: Discovered late after CSSOM
2
3<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/times-display.woff2"
4 as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin />
RIGHT: Preloaded on first HTML chunk
Font Request Timing: Late CSS Discovery vs Immediate HTML Preload
WRONG: DISCOVERED AT 1,400MS
TimesDisplay.woff2
✕ Request delayed until CSS parse finishes
RIGHT: PRELOADED AT 40MS
TimesDisplay.woff2
✓ High-priority fetch starts on first HTML chunk

A stylesheet link forces sequential waterfall penalties. The browser must resolve DNS, establish TLS, download the stylesheet, parse its rules, and attach elements to the render tree before realizing that the TimesDisplay font file is required. By adding <link rel="preload" as="font">, developers elevate the font file to high priority at the very beginning of the network stream. The crossorigin attribute is mandatory because web fonts are fetched using anonymous CORS requests according to web platform specifications; omitting it causes the browser to fetch the font twice.

Chrome Developers document this critical behavior in the official web performance guidance:

Fonts are often large files with slow load times. Some browsers hide text until the font loads, causing a flash of invisible text (FOIT).

Chrome Developers, Ensure text remains visible during webfont load, resources/web-performance/developer-chrome/site/en/docs/lighthouse/performance/font-display/index.md

Key Takeaway

Content visibility always trumps brand typography; render text immediately using local fallbacks and preload critical fonts to minimize swap shift.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: contrast all five font-display values (auto, block, swap, fallback, and optional). Highlight that font-display: optional provides the cleanest Core Web Vitals outcome on cellular connections: it gives the custom font a tiny 100ms block window and no swap window, meaning if the font is not in cache or cannot arrive almost instantly, the browser sticks with the fallback for that page view and caches the font for future visits, completely eliminating layout shift.

Where you will meet this

  • Breaking news portals: ensuring urgent headlines are readable within milliseconds on mobile networks.
  • E-commerce product catalogs: keeping pricing tags and call-to-action buttons instantly visible during flash sales.
  • Search result feeds: avoiding layout shifts and visual stutter when rendering dense snippets of information.

Glossary

  • Flash of Invisible Text (FOIT): A rendering state where text content remains completely invisible while the browser waits for a custom web font to download.
  • Flash of Unstyled Text (FOUT): A brief visual transition where text appears in a local system fallback font before swapping to the newly downloaded custom font.
  • font-display: A CSS @font-face descriptor controlling how font faces are rendered depending on whether and when they have finished downloading.
  • Preload Scanner: A secondary browser parser that scans incoming raw HTML streams to opportunistically discover and request critical resources like fonts and scripts.

Summary

Web Font Loading and FOIT Elimination

Web font optimization requires balancing brand typography with instant text accessibility.

❒ Loading Directives

  1. Font Display States
        (a) Block: hides text up to three seconds while awaiting external network font bytes.
        (b) Swap: paints local fallback instantly and replaces it when the custom font arrives.
        (c) Optional: avoids layout shift by aborting swap if the font is not cached or immediate.
  2. Network Discovery
        (a) Preload: initiates font download during initial HTML tokenization before CSS evaluation.
        (b) Crossorigin: ensures anonymous CORS credentials match web font specification requirements.

DO NOT DO THIS: Hide content behind blank delays using default font blocking.

index.html
1<link rel="stylesheet" href="/fonts.css">

    DO THIS: Render fallbacks immediately and preload the critical font file.

index.html
1<link rel="preload" href="/font.woff2"
2 as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

➔ NEVER allow article headlines to render invisibly while waiting for custom web fonts.

➔ ALWAYS supply crossorigin on font preload tags to prevent duplicate network downloads.

➔ IF a layout cannot tolerate visual reflow THEN configure font-display: optional on mobile.

DEFAULT BLOCK
(invisible text)		SWAP & PRELOAD
(immediate text)
Initial visibilityBlank empty spaces;
FOIT lasts up to 3s		Immediate readable text
via local system font
User comprehensionBlocked until external
network bytes arrive		Instant reading without
network dependencies
Discovery timingLate waterfall after
CSSOM construction		Instant high priority
via <link rel="preload">
Network efficiencyStalls render on poor
mobile connections		Smooth transition using
modern WOFF2 files
Layout stabilitySudden text pop-in
causes severe shift		Controlled fallback with
font metric overrides

Lecture 40: HTTP Caching: Headers, Revalidation, and Cache Busting

Interview Question

CORE

How do HTTP caching headers work, and what is cache busting?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Elena deploys a critical hotfix to resolve a broken subscription checkout script.
  2. Returning readers continue reporting checkout crashes because their browsers execute yesterday's cached JavaScript file.
  3. Why does the browser execute stale, broken scripts when updated code exists on the origin server?
  4. Readers cannot complete purchases, and support queues flood with duplicate billing complaints.
  5. The server shipped the asset with a long expiration header using an unversioned file path.
  6. HTTP caching must pair immutable cache lifetimes with content-hashed file URLs to guarantee instant updates.

The Stale Script Trap: Why Unversioned Assets Break Releases

Browsers maintain an HTTP disk and memory cache to prevent redundant network round trips on repeat visits. When an asset response includes a Cache-Control header with a high max-age directive, the browser assumes the file contents will remain valid for that duration. If the server serves a file at an unvarying URL like /js/checkout.js, the browser never contacts the origin server to verify whether newer code exists. Deploying an urgent bug fix to the same URL leaves existing users stranded on broken client logic:

response-headers.txt
1Cache-Control: max-age=31536000
WRONG: Locks /checkout.js in browser cache for 1 year
2
3Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable
RIGHT: Paired with unique content-hashed filename
Asset Versioning: Unversioned Script Lock vs Content-Hashed Update
WRONG: CACHED FOR 1 YEAR
checkout.js
✕ Stale script locked · Hotfix ignored
RIGHT: CONTENT HASH URL
checkout.8f3a.js
✓ New URL fetched instantly · Bug eliminated

The contrast illustrates why static asset caching requires content-based cache busting. On the left, giving an unversioned asset a one-year cache lifetime instructs the browser to bypass the network completely. Even if Elena restarts origin servers and purges upstream reverse proxies, returning subscribers load the buggy file directly from their local disk. On the right, modern bundlers append a cryptographic hash of the file contents to the filename, yielding /js/checkout.8f3a.js. Because any code modification alters the hash and produces a brand-new URL, the browser treats the asset as an entirely new resource, pulling the hotfix instantly while allowing untouched bundles to remain cached indefinitely.

The Gateway Document: Why HTML Must Never Be Cached Long-Term

Content-hashed static assets depend entirely on the document that references them. If the HTML page itself is cached by the browser, the browser will continue reading the older HTML markup, which still points to the superseded asset URLs. Therefore, HTML documents must always be configured with revalidation directives such as Cache-Control: no-cache. This directive does not prevent caching; instead, it mandates that the browser must validate freshness with the origin server before using the cached response:

html-headers.txt
1Cache-Control: max-age=86400
WRONG: Caches HTML for 24 hours, locking obsolete script URLs
2
3Cache-Control: no-cache
RIGHT: Mandates ETag revalidation on every single page load
HTML Caching: Stale 24-Hour Cache vs Instant ETag Revalidation
WRONG: MAX-AGE=86400
/checkout.html
✕ Clings to old script hash for 24 hours
RIGHT: NO-CACHE (ETAG 304)
/checkout.html
✓ Instant revalidation · Fetches fresh hashes

The difference between no-cache and no-store is one of the most widely misunderstood distinctions in web engineering. The directive no-store completely forbids any device or intermediary from saving the response to disk or memory, which is essential for sensitive banking or authentication endpoints. Conversely, no-cache allows the browser to store the HTML response locally, but requires an HTTP conditional request using If-None-Match and an ETag token. If the HTML has not changed, the origin server returns a lightweight 304 Not Modified status with an empty body, consuming zero layout overhead while ensuring new script hashes are discovered the instant they deploy.

Chrome Developers outline the foundational mechanic of client-side HTTP caching in the official audit documentation:

When a browser requests a resource, the server providing the resource can tell the browser how long it should temporarily store or cache the resource. For any subsequent request for that resource, the browser uses its local copy rather than getting it from the network.

Chrome Developers, Serve static assets with an efficient cache policy, resources/web-performance/developer-chrome/site/en/docs/lighthouse/performance/uses-long-cache-ttl/index.md

Key Takeaway

Pair immutable one-year cache headers on content-hashed static assets with no-cache conditional revalidation on root HTML documents.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: explain the immutable directive introduced in RFC 8246. When a user manually presses the browser reload button, standard browser behavior sends conditional revalidation requests for subresources even if their max-age has not expired. Appending immutable to Cache-Control informs modern browsers that the content will never change across its lifetime, suppressing conditional network requests completely during user reloads.

Where you will meet this

  • Continuous deployment pipelines: pushing code multiple times daily without invalidating untouched vendor libraries.
  • Single-page application shells: ensuring updated route bundles are downloaded immediately while assets stay cached.
  • Content delivery networks: configuring edge TTLs to offload origin servers while respecting client validation tokens.

Glossary

  • Cache-Control: An HTTP header used to specify browser and intermediary caching policies across request-response cycles.
  • Cache Busting: The engineering practice of appending unique content hashes or query tokens to asset URLs to force cache invalidation.
  • no-cache: A caching directive specifying that cached copies must be revalidated with the origin server before every reuse.
  • no-store: A caching directive strictly prohibiting browsers and proxy intermediaries from persisting responses to disk or memory.
  • ETag: An HTTP response header providing a cryptographic validator fingerprint used to determine if a cached entity matches origin state.

Summary

HTTP Caching Headers and Cache Busting

Effective caching pairs long-term static persistence with strict root revalidation.

❒ Caching Directives

  1. Static Asset Strategy
        (a) Hashed Bundles: set max-age=31536000 and immutable on content-hashed file names.
        (b) Content Invalidation: any source code edit changes the filename, bypassing old cache.
  2. Root Document Strategy
        (a) HTML Revalidation: set no-cache to force ETag verification on each page request.
        (b) Sensitive Data: set no-store on authenticated account and billing payloads.

DO NOT DO THIS: Cache static assets without content hashes or cache root HTML long-term.

index.html
1<script src="/js/app.js"></script>

    DO THIS: Reference content-hashed script bundles inside non-cached HTML shells.

index.html
1<script src="/js/app.d4e2.js"></script>

➔ NEVER assign long max-age durations to unversioned static URLs.

➔ ALWAYS serve root HTML documents with Cache-Control: no-cache to ensure rapid updates.

➔ IF an asset contains unique build hashes THEN mark it immutable for maximum efficiency.

(revalidated triad)

/js/checkout.js		Cryptographic hash;
/js/checkout.8f3a.js

accidental stale lock		max-age=31536000
paired with immutable
Hotfix deploymentFails for cached users;
requires manual hard purge		Instant pickup as HTML
points to brand-new URL
HTML cache ruleStatically cached,
prolonging stale pointers		no-cache ETag pass,
revalidating on each load

trips or broken apps		Zero redundant bytes;
unchanged bundles persist

Lecture 41: Payload Compression: Gzip Versus Brotli

Interview Question

CORE

What is the difference between gzip and Brotli, and what should you compress?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Leo monitors network performance on the morning financial market feed.
  2. The mobile client stalls for several seconds while downloading a massive financial update payload.
  3. Why does a text dataset of stock quotes take seconds to stream across a high-speed cellular link?
  4. Readers experience delayed market alerts, and data costs surge for mobile subscribers.
  5. The web server transmits raw, uncompressed text tokens without transport-layer encoding.
  6. Modern HTTP compression transforms redundant text payloads into compact bitstreams before wire transmission.

The Bloated Wire: How Uncompressed Text Chokes Connections

Web applications frequently exchange large volumes of textual data, including HTML documents, CSS stylesheets, JavaScript bundles, and JSON API responses. Because source code and structured data rely on repetitive keywords, tags, and whitespace, raw text files exhibit high information redundancy. When a web server delivers these assets without transport-layer compression, the client must download every single character verbatim across the physical network:

response-headers.txt
1Content-Type: application/json
WRONG: Raw uncompressed 2MB text stream over wire
2
3Content-Encoding: br
RIGHT: Brotli compressed stream reduces transfer size by 82%
Wire Transfer Payload: Uncompressed Text vs Brotli Stream
WRONG: 2.0MB RAW TEXT
market-feed.json
✕ 4.6s transfer on 3G · Radio stalls
RIGHT: 340KB BROTLI (BR)
market-feed.json
✓ 0.8s transfer on 3G · Fast response

The contrast demonstrates the profound impact of wire compression on mobile user retention. On the left, streaming two megabytes of raw text across a high-latency cellular network saturates the device's radio buffer and delays DOM processing. On the right, enabling Brotli compression shrinks the payload down to 340 kilobytes. Because HTTP compression occurs transparently at the transport layer, the browser automatically decodes the stream back into its original text representation before handing it to the JavaScript engine, preserving total code fidelity while cutting download times by more than eighty percent.

The Algorithmic Edge: Gzip, Brotli, and What Never to Compress

For decades, gzip served as the standard web compression format, combining LZ77 sliding-window dictionary matching with Huffman entropy coding across a thirty-two-kilobyte window. Brotli represents a major architectural leap designed specifically for the web. In addition to dynamic dictionary compression with sliding windows up to sixteen megabytes, Brotli incorporates a built-in static dictionary containing over thirteen thousand common strings, including HTML tags, standard CSS properties, and ubiquitous JavaScript boilerplate:

nginx.conf
1gzip_types text/plain image/jpeg; # **WRONG:** Wastes server CPU compressing compressed JPEG
2
3brotli_types text/html application/json; # **RIGHT:** Compresses text and structured data only
Compression Scope: Double-Compressing Media vs Text-Only Target
WRONG: GZIPPED WEBP IMAGE
/photos/hero.webp
✕ CPU waste · Zero reduction (+30 bytes)
RIGHT: BROTLI JAVASCRIPT
/js/bundle.js
✓ 78% reduction · Saves 850KB on wire

A common infrastructure anti-pattern involves attempting to compress binary media files. Media formats such as JPEG, WebP, AVIF, MP4, and WOFF2 already employ specialized, highly optimized compression algorithms tailored to image, video, and font data. Forcing an already compressed binary file through Gzip or Brotli yields virtually zero byte savings, burns expensive server and client CPU cycles, and can even increase the final file size due to compression header overhead. Web compression must be strictly reserved for text-based assets: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG, XML, and JSON.

The Mozilla Developer Network defines the computational mechanics of modern Brotli compression:

Brotli is a general-purpose lossless compression algorithm. It compresses data using a combination of a modern variant of the Lempel-Ziv coding LZ77 algorithm, Huffman coding, and second-order context modeling, providing a compression ratio comparable to the best currently available general-purpose compression methods.

MDN Web Docs, Brotli compression, resources/web-performance/mdn/files/en-us/glossary/brotli_compression/index.md

Key Takeaway

Always enable Brotli for text-based assets, keep Gzip as an HTTP fallback, and never compress pre-compressed binary media.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: discuss the difference between static pre-compression and dynamic on-the-fly compression. For static build assets (production JS, CSS, and HTML), run Brotli at maximum compression level 11 ahead of time during the CI build; because compression happens once at compile time, the CPU cost is irrelevant, but users reap the smallest possible byte payloads. For dynamic API responses generated on the fly, configure compression at levels 4 to 6 to strike the optimal balance between CPU latency and byte reduction.

Where you will meet this

  • Edge proxy gateways: automatically negotiating Accept-Encoding: br, gzip between client browsers and backends.
  • Build asset pipelines: pre-compressing static JavaScript chunks into .br and .gz archives during deployment.
  • High-frequency API endpoints: compressing JSON payloads to keep mobile device radio transmission windows brief.

Glossary

  • Gzip: A widely supported lossless compression format combining LZ77 and Huffman coding with a 32KB sliding window.
  • Brotli: A modern lossless compression algorithm utilizing LZ77, Huffman coding, and a predefined 13KB static web dictionary.
  • Content-Encoding: An HTTP header indicating what compression algorithm was applied to the transmitted response entity.
  • Accept-Encoding: An HTTP request header sent by the browser advertising which compression algorithms it supports.
  • Static Pre-compression: The practice of compressing assets ahead of time during the build process to eliminate runtime CPU overhead.

Summary

Payload Compression: Gzip Versus Brotli

Wire compression drastically reduces download latency by stripping redundancy from text assets.

❒ Compression Mechanics

  1. Algorithm Comparison
        (a) Gzip: universal compatibility; uses a 32KB sliding dictionary window.
        (b) Brotli: 14% to 25% denser than gzip on web text; uses a 13KB static web dictionary.
  2. Compression Targets
        (a) Target Text: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG, JSON, and XML.
        (b) Exclude Binaries: never compress JPEG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, WOFF2, or MP4.

DO NOT DO THIS: Enable compression filters on binary images or fonts.

nginx.conf
1gzip_types text/html image/png font/woff2;

    DO THIS: Target text assets and pre-compress static bundles in your CI build.

nginx.conf
1brotli_types text/html text/css application/json;

➔ NEVER run compression algorithms on pre-compressed image or video assets.

➔ ALWAYS pre-compress static assets using Brotli level 11 during the production build.

➔ IF serving dynamic JSON endpoints THEN tune compression levels to avoid CPU bottlenecks.

(modern web default)

plus Huffman coding		LZ77, second-order context,
plus static dictionary

window memory limit		Sliding window up to 16MB
plus 13KB web vocabulary

assets by ~70%		Superior; 14% to 25%
smaller than gzip

older HTTP clients		Gold standard for static
production JS and CSS
Non-text behaviorBurns CPU without gain
on binary formats		Burns CPU without gain

Lecture 42: Content Delivery Networks: Latency and Edge Routing

Interview Question

CORE

Why do CDNs matter, and how does distance affect latency?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Chloe opens the National Times morning podcast stream from her apartment in Sydney, Australia.
  2. The playback controls spin for four agonizing seconds before the first audio segment begins playing.
  3. Why does connecting to an online media stream take four seconds on a high-speed fiber connection?
  4. International subscribers encounter stalled streams, and audio buffering prompts immediate churn.
  5. Every network packet must physically cross undersea cables to a single origin server in Virginia.
  6. Content Delivery Networks position edge servers globally to eliminate the speed-of-light propagation penalty.

The Tyranny of Distance: Why Bandwidth Cannot Fix Latency

High-bandwidth fiber internet connections can transfer gigabytes of data every minute, but they cannot alter the fundamental laws of physics. Light travels through optical fiber at approximately two hundred kilometers per millisecond. When a user in Australia connects to a web server located in North America, a single round trip covers over thirty thousand kilometers of fiber and routing hops, imposing an irreducible round-trip time (RTT) of nearly three hundred milliseconds:

audio-player.html
1<audio src="https://origin-va.times.com/brief.mp3"></audio>
WRONG: 16,000 km to Virginia (280ms RTT)
2
3<audio src="https://cdn.times.com/brief.mp3"></audio>
RIGHT: 25 km to Sydney edge PoP (12ms RTT)
Global Audio Stream: Virginia Origin vs Edge Point of Presence
WRONG: VIRGINIA ORIGIN SERVER
Daily Briefing Audio
✕ 4,200ms connection delay (280ms RTT)
RIGHT: SYDNEY CDN EDGE NODE
Daily Briefing Audio
✓ 48ms connection delay (12ms RTT)

The contrast reveals why physical proximity dominates connection startup speed. Before a single audio byte can stream from Virginia, the browser must execute DNS resolution, a TCP three-way handshake, and a TLS cryptographic negotiation. Across a 280-millisecond RTT, completing these preliminary handshakes consumes over one full second of total latency without transferring any application data. Under TCP slow-start, ramping up throughput requires several additional round trips. A Content Delivery Network (CDN) solves this by maintaining Points of Presence (PoPs) worldwide, allowing Chloe's browser to terminate network handshakes with a local edge server located just twelve milliseconds away in Sydney.

Edge Termination: Accelerating Dynamic Requests Across the Globe

While CDNs are widely recognized for caching static images and media files, their architecture delivers equal benefits for dynamic, uncacheable API transactions. When an edge server receives an uncacheable request, it terminates the client's TCP and TLS sessions locally in the subscriber's home region. The CDN then proxies the request to the origin server across an optimized private fiber backbone using persistent, pre-warmed TCP connections:

edge-headers.txt
1Host: origin-va.times.com
WRONG: Client negotiates raw TLS over public internet across globe
2
3Host: edge-syd.times.com
RIGHT: Edge terminates TLS in Sydney and routes over warm backbone
Edge Architecture: Distant Origin Handshake vs Edge TLS Termination
WRONG: GLOBAL ORIGIN (4 RTTS)
TLS Cryptographic Pass
✕ 1,120ms multi-hop negotiation
RIGHT: EDGE POP (4 RTTS)
TLS Cryptographic Pass
✓ 48ms local connection setup

Terminating network protocols at the edge fundamentally transforms user experience. In traditional architectures, packet loss occurring anywhere along a ten-thousand-mile route forces a full-distance TCP retransmission timeout. In a CDN edge topology, packet recovery occurs locally over the reliable last-mile connection. Furthermore, CDN providers deploy anycast DNS routing to steer user traffic to the geographically or topologically closest edge facility, insulating origin data centers from traffic spikes and distributed denial-of-service attacks while keeping global response times uniform.

Ilya Grigorik defines the geometric necessity of global CDN infrastructure in the web performance literature:

Content delivery network (CDN) services provide many benefits, but chief among them is the simple observation that distributing the content around the globe, and serving that content from a nearby location to the client, enables us to significantly reduce the propagation time of all the data packets. We may not be able to make the packets travel faster, but we can reduce the distance by strategically positioning our servers closer to the users!

Ilya Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking, resources/web-performance/hpbn/primer-on-latency-and-bandwidth/index.html

Key Takeaway

You cannot accelerate the speed of light; move computing resources and cache layers physically closer to users via edge points of presence.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: explain Anycast BGP routing. Rather than assigning a distinct IP address to every edge server in every city, an anycast CDN announces the exact same IP prefix from hundreds of data centers worldwide. Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) routers across the internet automatically route each client's packets along the shortest autonomous system path to the nearest operating edge node, providing automated failover and regional load shedding.

Where you will meet this

  • Global media streaming: distributing high-resolution audio and video segments without international buffering delays.
  • Mobile banking interfaces: completing secure TLS handshakes at local edge nodes to speed up fund transfer confirmations.
  • Breaking international news: absorbing massive global traffic spikes when a worldwide headline breaks simultaneously.

Glossary

  • Content Delivery Network (CDN): A geographically distributed network of proxy servers and data centers that serve content to users from nearby locations.
  • Point of Presence (PoP): A physical access point and location where CDN edge servers interface with local internet service provider networks.
  • Round-Trip Time (RTT): The duration in milliseconds required for a network data packet to travel from a sender to a destination and return.
  • Edge Termination: The architectural practice of terminating TCP and TLS cryptographic handshakes at a nearby proxy node rather than the distant origin.
  • Anycast: A network addressing and routing technique where a single IP address is shared and routed across multiple physical server locations.

Summary

Content Delivery Networks: Latency and Edge Routing

Distance is the fundamental enemy of web speed; edge deployment eliminates propagation lag.

❒ CDN Capabilities

  1. Latency Reduction
        (a) Physical Proximity: reduces round-trip times from hundreds of milliseconds to under 20ms.
        (b) Connection Warmup: terminates DNS, TCP, and TLS handshakes at the local edge PoP.
  2. Dynamic Acceleration
        (a) Backbone Routing: ferries uncached API traffic across private optimized backbones.
        (b) Origin Shielding: collapses multiple redundant edge requests into single origin fetches.

DO NOT DO THIS: Force international users to connect directly to a single distant origin.

index.html
1<img src="https://us-east-1.times.com/hero.jpg">

    DO THIS: Route all static and media assets through a globally distributed CDN.

index.html
1<img src="https://cdn.times.com/hero.jpg">

➔ NEVER ignore physical geography when designing response latency budgets.

➔ ALWAYS terminate TLS and TCP handshakes at edge Points of Presence.

➔ IF serving dynamic APIs to global users THEN leverage CDN backbone acceleration.

Lecture 43: Bundle Size: Code Splitting and Tree Shaking

Interview Question

CORE

How do you manage bundle size with code splitting and tree shaking?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Maya opens an investigative news article on her phone to read a transit story.
  2. The reading view freezes for several seconds while the phone's mobile processor overheats.
  3. Why does reading a plain text article require downloading and compiling a massive charting suite?
  4. The battery drains rapidly, mobile data plans are exhausted, and readers abandon the site.
  5. The build system bundled every administrative and visualization tool into a single monolithic script.
  6. Modern module bundlers must split code into dynamic chunks and eliminate unused exports through tree shaking.

The Monolithic Penalty: Why Shipping Everything Upfront Fails

In single-page applications and content sites, developers frequently import external utility libraries and visualization frameworks. When build tools bundle all application routes into a single monolithic script file, every reader is forced to download, parse, and compile code for features they may never encounter. An article reader seeking a simple text report ends up downloading heavy data visualization suites intended solely for interactive dashboards:

article-view.js
1import { HeavyChartSuite } from 'all-charts';
WRONG: 850KB charting bundle loaded on plain text page
2
3const { renderChart } = await import('./chart.js');
RIGHT: 18KB chunk loaded on demand when user clicks
Article Initialization: Monolithic Bundle vs Dynamic Import
WRONG: 850KB MONOLITHIC BUNDLE
Transit Report
✕ 1,800ms main thread lockup
RIGHT: 45KB ROUTE CORE
Transit Report
✓ 40ms instant article render

The contrast demonstrates how initial bundle weight damages perceived performance. JavaScript is vastly more expensive than media because it consumes main thread CPU time during the critical startup phase. On mid-tier smartphones, compiling 850 kilobytes of code locks the browser for nearly two seconds, creating frozen buttons and ragged scroll physics. Dynamic imports using import() split the dependency tree into isolated chunks. The browser downloads the lightweight core text route immediately, postponing the charting package until the user explicitly toggles the interactive visualization.

Static Analysis: Shaking Dead Code from Production Bundles

In addition to splitting routes, applications must eliminate unused helper methods from imported packages. Traditional CommonJS modules use dynamic require() statements, which prevent compilers from determining which functions are actually called prior to runtime execution. Modern ECMAScript Modules (ESM) utilize static import and export syntax, allowing bundlers like Rollup and Webpack to analyze the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) and prune unreferenced code from production output:

utils.js
1const _ = require('lodash');
WRONG: CommonJS dynamic require bundles entire 72KB library
2
3import { debounce } from 'lodash-es';
RIGHT: Static ESM import shakes out 70KB of unused functions
Dead Code Elimination: Whole Library Import vs Shaken Export
WRONG: FULL LODASH (72KB)
Vendor Utility Bundle
✕ 300 unused methods packaged
RIGHT: SHAKEN DEBOUNCE (2KB)
Vendor Utility Bundle
✓ 70KB dead code eliminated

Tree shaking relies strictly on static structure. When an application imports a single named export from an ES module, the bundler traces the import graph and discards untouched methods, shrinking the utility payload from seventy kilobytes down to two. However, tree shaking fails if libraries contain unflagged module-level side effects, such as mutating global prototypes or executing logging loops during import. To ensure optimal shaking, package authors must declare "sideEffects": false in their package.json, signaling to bundlers that unreferenced files within the package can be pruned safely.

Google web performance engineers define the core objective of code splitting in the official guidance:

Code splitting is a technique that seeks to minimize startup time. When we ship less JavaScript at startup, we can get applications to be interactive faster by minimizing main thread work during this critical period.

Houssein Djirdeh and Jeremy Wagner, Reduce JavaScript payloads with code splitting, resources/web-performance/web-dev/src/site/content/en/fast/reduce-javascript-payloads-with-code-splitting/index.md

Key Takeaway

Ship only the JavaScript required for the initial route; load heavy interactive modules on demand and prune dead exports with static ESM imports.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: explain how route-based code splitting interacts with the browser's preload scanner and resource hints. While dynamic import() prevents unnecessary code execution, waiting until a route click to initiate the fetch introduces navigation delay. Sophisticated architectures use <link rel="prefetch"> or hover-intent listeners to prefetch the next route chunk during idle browser cycles, combining tiny initial bundles with instantaneous page transitions.

Where you will meet this

  • Admin dashboards: isolating heavy report generators and CSV export libraries from the login screen.
  • Media newsrooms: lazy loading interactive election maps and polling charts only when users scroll them into view.
  • E-commerce checkouts: loading 3D product preview canvases asynchronously after the main catalog renders.

Glossary

  • Code Splitting: The process of dividing a single large application bundle into smaller chunks that can be loaded on demand or in parallel.
  • Tree Shaking: A dead code elimination technique that statically inspects ES module imports and exports to discard unused code from bundles.
  • Dynamic Import: The import() function syntax enabling asynchronous, on-demand loading of JavaScript modules during runtime.
  • Side Effects: Code that executes observable mutations outside its local scope, such as modifying global objects or setting timers during module evaluation.
  • Abstract Syntax Tree (AST): A hierarchical tree representation of the syntactic structure of source code used by compilers to analyze and transform programs.

Summary

Bundle Size: Code Splitting and Tree Shaking

Controlling bundle size preserves main thread responsiveness by shipping only immediate code.

❒ Bundle Optimization

  1. Code Splitting Methods
        (a) Route Splitting: isolate each application page into its own asynchronous bundle.
        (b) Component Splitting: defer heavy modals, rich editors, and complex charts via dynamic import.
  2. Tree Shaking Rules
        (a) Static ESM Syntax: use import and export statements to allow AST compile-time analysis.
        (b) Side Effect Flags: mark sideEffects: false in package.json to permit dead module elimination.

DO NOT DO THIS: Import monolithic libraries globally across the primary entrypoint.

app.js
1import * as Analytics from 'monolith-analytics-suite';

    DO THIS: Import named ES modules statically or load heavy modules dynamically.

app.js
1import { trackView } from 'monolith-analytics-suite/view';

➔ NEVER bundle heavy administrative or visualization tools into the primary reading route.

➔ ALWAYS use static ECMAScript Module imports instead of dynamic CommonJS require syntax.

➔ IF a component is below the fold or hidden in a modal THEN load it via dynamic import().

MONOLITHIC BUNDLE

(modular on-demand chunks)

unnecessary code		Minimal route shell;
under 50KB core JS
Main thread impactHeavy parse and compile
blocks user taps		Instant evaluation;
silky smooth INP score

dormant functions		Pruned from output via
static AST analysis
